cards.explanation: The answer is burned. The text says the Amalekites "…had raided the Negev, attacked Ziklag, and burned it down." That's a whole town gone, and I once scorched a single batch and felt terrible. David's men come home to this, friends, so I'll keep my burnt cookie complaints to myself.

The answer is False. The text says, "They had not killed anyone, but had carried them off as they went on their way." The people were taken captive, both young and old. That matters, friends, because captives can still be found.

The answer is that they weep until they have no strength left. David and his troops "…lifted up their voices and wept until they had no strength left to weep." These are soldiers, friends, and they cry until there's nothing left. I think that part is just plain heartbreaking, and I'm not going to joke about it.

The answer is Abigail, the widow of Nabal of Carmel. The text names David's two captive wives as Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail. These two aren't just names on a list, friends. They're the people David is about to go after.

The answer is stoning David. The text says David was greatly distressed "…because the people spoke of stoning him…" These are men who just lost their sons and daughters, and they aim all that pain at their leader. I think David is hurting plenty on his own, and now his own people are muttering about stones.

The answer is in the LORD his God. "But David found strength in the LORD his God." Look at the timing, friends. His town is burned, his family is gone, and his own men are talking about stoning him, and the text says he finds his strength in the LORD.

The answer is True. David tells Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, "Bring me the ephod." So Abiathar brought it to him, and then "…David inquired of the LORD…" Once the ephod is there, friends, David turns to the LORD with his questions.

The answer is that the LORD tells him to pursue, and he will rescue the captives. David asks, "Should I pursue these raiders? Will I overtake them?" and the LORD answers, "Pursue them, for you will surely overtake them and rescue the captives." David asks two questions and gets a full yes to both. When the LORD tells you to go, friends, you can go.

The answer is two hundred. The text says "…two hundred men were too exhausted to cross the brook." That leaves David with four hundred to keep going. I bet exhaustion hits hard after that kind of heartbreak.

The answer is False. Two hundred men were too exhausted to cross the brook, "But David and four hundred men continued in pursuit." He keeps moving, friends. The two hundred stay behind at the Brook of Besor.

The answer is False, friends. The text says David's men found an Egyptian in the field and brought him to David. Then "They gave the man water to drink and food to eat…" Nothing in the verse says anyone tied him up.

The answer is three days and three nights. The text says "…he had not had any food or water for three days and three nights." Then he gets a piece of a fig cake and two clusters of raisins, and he's revived. After that long, friends, I think a fig cake would taste like the finest thing in the world.

The answer is an Amalekite. The man says, "I am an Egyptian," and that he is "the slave of an Amalekite." That's the same people who raided Ziklag. So David is talking to someone who knows exactly where the raiders went.

The answer is False. The man says, "My master abandoned me three days ago when I fell ill." It was illness, friends, and nothing about escaping. I think that's a sad way to be treated, and it leaves him wanting help.

The answer is that he asks David not to kill him or hand him over. He says, "Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or deliver me into the hand of my master, and I will lead you to them." He's already been left behind once, so I think he wants a promise before he trusts anyone. In return he'll lead David right to the raiders.

The answer is eating and celebrating their plunder. The Amalekites were "…eating, drinking, and celebrating the great amount of plunder they had taken from the land of the Philistines and the land of Judah." They're spread out and having a party, friends. That's a whole lot of plunder to celebrate.

The answer is False. The text says, "Not a man escaped, except four hundred young men who fled, riding off on camels." Four hundred got away, friends. It's a big fight, and it still has that one exception.

The answer is all of it, friends. "…David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken, including his two wives." The text adds, "Nothing was missing, young or old, son or daughter, or any of the plunder the Amalekites had taken." Every person and every bit of plunder came back.

The answer is to give them only their wives and children. Those men say, "Because they did not go with us, we will not share with them the plunder we recovered, except for each man’s wife and children. They may take them and go." The text calls them "…wicked and worthless men…" They want to cut the exhausted ones out of the plunder completely, friends.

The answer is that the LORD gave it and protected them. David says, "…you must not do this with what the LORD has given us. He has protected us and delivered into our hands the raiders who came against us." So the plunder is a gift from the LORD, friends, and it isn't something to hoard. David puts the credit where it belongs.

The answer is match. David says, "The share of the one who went to battle will match the share of the one who stayed with the supplies. They will share alike." Same share for both, friends. Whoever watched the supplies gets the same as whoever fought.

The answer is True, friends. The text says, "And so it has been from that day forward. David established this statute and ordinance for Israel to this very day." That ruling was that the two groups "…will share alike." I think that's a rule worth keeping around.

The answer is elders. The text says David sent some of the plunder "…to his friends, the elders of Judah, saying…" The message was, "Here is a gift for you from the plunder of the LORD’s enemies." The writer calls them his friends, friends. I think that's a generous way to share.
